articleRohrbeck.title: Why Rohrbeck FITness Still Matters
articleRohrbeck.subtitle: Future Readiness is not enough; organizations must perceive, prospect, and probe.
articleRohrbeck.body:
In management meetings we often hear “we have a foresight unit” or “our Future Readiness score is high.” Then a crisis hits and the same monthly reports land on the table. The brutal question follows: why does your foresight fail at the moment of decision?

Many organizations discover this is not a lack of reports. Reports exist, workshops happened, slides were shown. The problem is that foresight has been documentation, not live capability. It resembles shallow country comparisons: they look scientific until a crisis exposes the missing context.

René Rohrbeck’s Future FITness model draws the line. Readiness means “we are prepared.” FITness means “we are actively adjusting to the future.” The gap sounds subtle; in practice it is enormous. One produces documents; the other tests new paths.

when foresight is only performance

In many firms, foresight becomes an annual event: a trend report, a few AI slides, applause, and a return to the same operating loop. Perceiving, Prospecting, and Probing are missing. There is “seeing” without exploring or probing.

Cases at Siemens and Deutsche Telekom show foresight lives when tied to technology radar, venturing, and investment decisions. When it only decorates board meetings, it becomes beautiful, convincing, and useless.

three processes, five dimensions

Perceiving means catching weak signals and structural shifts. Prospecting means exploring possible paths, not one linear forecast. Probing means pilots, ventures, and small experiments that test the future instead of only talking about it.

Five maturity dimensions (culture, structure, process, resources, output) separate reporting theater from real capability. Without foresight culture, the best report goes to the shelf. Without venturing structure, probing cannot happen. One weak dimension collapses the whole system into performance.

alive or documented?

FITness still matters because it answers the opening question. If your foresight only works in calm times and goes silent in crisis, you have Readiness, not FITness. If the team reports but nothing reaches the market as a probe, your foresight is documented, not alive.

Ask yourself: when did foresight last change a real decision? If the answer is hard to find, the problem is not tools; it is architecture. FITness is a navigation map, not a decorative label.

articleCla.title: What CLA Sees Before Policy
articleCla.subtitle: Before policy comes discourse and myth; CLA makes them visible.
articleCla.body:
A new policy is announced. A task force forms, data is collected, a document is drafted. Yet some options never reach the table. Even with “scientific” analysis, the debate returns to the same menu. Why?

That question is the heart of CLA. Sohail Inayatullah’s Causal Layered Analysis shows that policy takes shape in deeper layers before any clause is written. If you only see the surface, it is like reading a scoreboard and thinking you know the whole game.

the Litany trap

Policymakers and media usually work at the Litany layer: numbers, crises, headlines, KPIs. That layer matters, but if we stop there, deeper causes and hidden worldviews stay invisible. Litany tells you what happened, not why only certain options feel thinkable.

Think of claims that “sport must stay separate from politics” while the framing, naming, and staging of an event is itself precise social engineering. The surface looks neutral; deeper layers already defined the game.

four layers, one picture

Systemic opens structures: law, markets, infrastructure, incentives. Worldview opens assumptions: “growth is always good,” “the state must control,” “technology fixes itself.” Myth/Metaphor opens the stories that limit debate: hero, victim, golden return, absolute binaries.

CLA says that until metaphor shifts, the policy menu does not shift. You can tweak numbers, but if the myth remains “all or nothing,” middle paths never become serious.

In Singapore and ASEAN, CLA reshapes conversation before the policy paper. When stakeholders move from Litany to Worldview and Myth, options appear that once seemed impossible. Here foresight and policy truly connect.

a pre-policy tool

CLA is a pre-policy tool. It explains why some options never reach the table, not which option is “correct.” If you want genuinely new policy, first see which discourse and myth already constrain it.

Ask: when did a policy meeting last discuss the Myth layer? If you always stay in Litany and Systemic, do not expect breakthrough. CLA is a flashlight for the layers that define the game before the law is written.

articleUncertainty.title: Navigating Uncertainty
articleUncertainty.subtitle: When we are unsure how sure we are, we need different tools.
articleUncertainty.body:
Two experts treat a weak signal seriously; two others say it is too early. Management wants one number, one decision, one direction. What do you do? Vote and move on?

This happens in foresight more often than we admit. Scenarios and critical uncertainties are powerful, but they hide an assumption: boundaries can be fixed. When judgments themselves are fuzzy, forcing a single probability is a strategic error.

manufacturing false certainty

In foresight sessions, a number often lands on the table: “0.7 probability,” “high confidence trend,” “medium-priority weak signal.” It looks scientific. Behind it, real expert disagreement is hidden. The person who said 0.7 might accept 0.4 to 0.8; the dissenter might dispute the definition of “emerging.”

That disagreement is part of reality, not method failure. In deep uncertainty, the boundary between “important” and “noise,” “likely” and “unlikely,” is itself fuzzy. Ignore that and your foresight becomes shallow simulation: a model that misrepresents the world.

Type-2 fuzzy logic

Lotfi Zadeh introduced Type-1 fuzzy logic for degrees of membership: a trend can be “somewhat” emerging. Type-2 goes further: it models uncertainty about the fuzzy boundaries themselves. Instead of one crisp membership function, you get a Footprint of Uncertainty (FOU); the model admits “we do not know exactly where the boundary is.”

In foresight this means saying “this trend is likely emerging” with a band of doubt, not a single 0.7 everyone must accept. For weak signals, expert disagreement, and decisions under ambiguity, that is often more honest than naive probability.

Example: a new AI technology. Team A sees a strong signal; Team B sees noise. Type-2 lets you say membership is high, but uncertainty about membership is also high. Management understands it should probe, not commit all-in.

do not hide ambiguity

Navigating uncertainty means choosing tools that do not fake certainty. The opening question remains: when even “how sure are we?” is disputed, the answer is the right tool.

If your foresight always delivers one clean number, it probably killed ambiguity instead of resolving it. In a world where weak signals matter, honesty about uncertainty beats fake precision. Type-2 fuzzy logic is technical language for a honesty that management meetings often lose.

articleAiTime.title: Beyond the Biological Clock
articleAiTime.subtitle: Time in the body, the organization, and the machine; three rhythms, not one.
articleAiTime.body:
A manager wants a large language model live next month. Engineering says weeks. Legal says years. HR says the workforce is not ready. Who is right?

If you accept only one timeline, someone must be “wrong.” But everyone may be right; they are talking about different clocks. That is where technology foresight often fails: forcing one biological clock on every team.

one calendar for humans and machines

Human circadian rhythm is slow and cyclical: focus, fatigue, weekly cadence. AI systems and cloud infrastructure count milliseconds. Organizations sit between: committees, approvals, budget cycles. Treat the three as one and you build lying roadmaps.

Many tech analyses compute “time to market” from technical latency alone. Social adoption, regulatory change, and organizational learning run on separate clocks. It is like saying that because the steam engine existed, whole societies should industrialize within a year.

three kinds of time in one analysis

In technology foresight, “time” is not just a timeline. Decision tempo (how fast you can commit), infrastructure latency (how fast you deploy), and social adoption rhythm (how long people and institutions accept change) are separate layers.

LLM deployment is a clear example: technically possible in weeks, pilot in months, compliance and trust in years. Fuzzy logic can model “slow,” “gradual,” and “sudden” without hard cutoffs; not a crisp 18 months, but a band from 6 to 36 with different confidence per layer.

If your foresight only sees the manager’s clock, engineering always looks slow and legal always looks heavy. Separate the three clocks and you see where the bottleneck is and where to place the probe.

hold several rhythms at once

Beyond the biological clock means seeing technical, organizational, and social time separately, then combining them. The opening question is answered: both sides can be right; they speak of different clocks.

For every emerging technology project, ask three questions: how long technically? how long for the organization to accept? how long for society and regulation? Answer only one and your foresight is incomplete. The future of technology is multi-temporal; foresight must be too.

articleHinesBishop.title: From Toolbox to Process
articleHinesBishop.subtitle: Hines and Bishop’s Six Pillars answer “what do I do now?”
articleHinesBishop.body:
FRM 3.0 offers 39 methods. A manager looks at the list and asks: where do I start? Run everything at once and foresight becomes a heavy, exhausting project; run nothing and it stays talk. That paradox is real for many organizations.

It resembles copying another country’s development model without asking which stage you are in and where the bottleneck sits. Plenty of tools, little architecture; the result is exhaustion or theater.

the toolbox trap

FRM 3.0 is a treasure chest: Delphi, scenarios, futures wheel, CLA, backcasting, and dozens more. A chest becomes a problem when you do not know which key opens which lock. Many organizations start with one big workshop, produce 200 pages, and never reach Acting.

Great Scanning without Visioning yields shelf reports. Strong Visioning without Acting yields management wallpaper. Forecasting without Framing answers a question nobody asked. Every FRM method has value, but without architecture it is random.

six pillars, one path

Andy Hines and Peter Bishop turned foresight into a process: Framing → Scanning → Forecasting → Visioning → Planning → Acting. Each pillar has a failure mode and a blunt question.

Framing: “Are we asking the right question?” Scanning: “Do we see the horizon or only read feeds?” Forecasting: “Do we have plausible futures or fantasy?” Visioning: “Do we share an image?” Planning: “Do we have a pathway?” Acting: “Has a probe reached the market?”

The Cone of Plausibility bridges Forecasting and Visioning; not every fantasy, only plausible futures. In Houston’s program and APF courses, once an organization knows which pillar is stuck, it picks FRM tools on purpose, not all at once.

you need architecture

A toolbox is not enough; you need architecture. “Where do I start?” gets an answer when you know which pillar you are in and which gap comes next.

If your foresight always starts with scanning but never reaches acting, the problem is not tools; it is pillars. Six Pillars is a navigation map: not 39 random methods, but a path from question to probe. FRM is the library; Six Pillars is the compass.

university.title: Popper Foresight Diamond · two lecture decks
university.intro: Based on Rafael Popper's Foresight Diamond from the EU FORLEARN projects, with a bridge to Michel Godet's five scenario quality criteria. The Diamond is not a prediction tool, it is a lens for judging the quality of a foresight exercise.

modules.title: Four corners of the diamond in practice
modules.lectureIntro: Session 1 of this module clarifies the four corners of the Popper Diamond, creativity, innovation, expertise, and interaction, using workshop examples so their exact meaning is clear before any audit.

lectureSections.title: 1. Why quality matters more than completion
slideTitles: A two hundred page report, still weak
The diamond versus a method list
paragraphs: Many foresight projects end with a long report without any clarity on whether that report was actually good, or merely completed.
Rafael Popper formalized this question in the EU FORLEARN projects: how do we know a foresight exercise was good, not just finished?
The FRM lists thirty nine methods but offers no tool for comparing their quality. The Popper Diamond is a meta-tool that applies across any method, from Delphi to scenarios.

lectureSections.title: 2. Creativity and innovation
slideTitles: Innovation: a new path or mere repetition
A weak example and a strong example
paragraphs: The creativity corner asks whether unexpected ideas, fresh metaphors, or an angle that did not exist before the workshop actually appeared.
The innovation corner goes one step further: did the workshop's output surface a new policy option, a new business model, or a new operational path?
A weak example is a workshop that simply relists already known trends. A strong example is a workshop that challenges one of the organization's core assumptions with a new metaphor.

lectureSections.title: 3. Expertise and interaction
slideTitles: A hollow corner as a quality warning
paragraphs: The expertise corner asks whether deep domain knowledge, citable evidence, and analytical competence sat behind the result, or only general guesswork.
The interaction corner shows the difference between a stakeholder who genuinely helped shape the result and one who merely signed the attendance sheet.
Popper stresses that weak foresight is usually completely hollow in one or two corners, for example high expertise with no real stakeholder interaction at all.

modules.title: Auditing foresight quality: from the diamond to Godet's criteria
modules.visualCaption: From workshop evidence to a management memo
modules.lectureIntro: Session 2 walks through the audit process step by step and places Godet's five scenario quality criteria alongside the Popper Diamond, forming a shared language for judging foresight quality.

lectureSections.title: 1. The audit process, step by step
paragraphs: The audit starts by gathering real workshop evidence: minutes, the final report, the participant list, and any other written output.

Each corner is scored against evidence, not a general impression. Interaction, for example, is measured by the number and diversity of stakeholders who genuinely contributed opinions, not by the headcount in the room.
The pattern of scores matters more than their average. A diamond with high expertise and every other corner low sends a different warning than a diamond with a medium score across all corners.

lectureSections.title: 2. Godet's five criteria as a complement
slideTitles: Strategic importance and transparency of method
paragraphs: Michel Godet proposes three criteria for judging scenario quality: direct relevance to the strategic question, internal narrative coherence, and plausibility within existing knowledge.

Godet's other two criteria are the strategic importance of the result for the decision maker and transparency of the method used, a criterion that connects directly to the expertise corner of the Popper Diamond.
Godet's criteria are sharper for scenario content, and the Popper Diamond is broader for workshop process. Using both together makes an audit sensitive to product and to process at once.

lectureSections.title: 3. A redesign case and a management memo
slideTitles: Case: a ministry and a two round Delphi
From audit to a redesign proposal
A one page memo for the board
paragraphs: In a real Delphi workshop, expertise scored high while creativity and innovation scored low. The audit showed the problem was not the method itself, but the absence of room for unexpected ideas.
The redesign proposal added one CLA or scenario session before the second Delphi round, rather than repeating the same method and hoping for a better result.
The final audit output is a one page memo: the four corner scores, the related Godet criterion, and one clear recommendation, ready before a board presentation.

modules.title: Six pillars: an architecture for strategic foresight
modules.visualCaption: From framing to acting, one chain
modules.lectureIntro: This page is the map of the six pillars plus Framework Foresight. Opening slides say why the path exists; then you see the depth of each column. Each column below is its own deck.

lectureSections.imageCaption: Six pillars as a manager path
lectureSections.title: 1. From method list to path
paragraphs:
M0 is the orientation deck. It shows why the six pillars form one chain before you open any single column.

Use it when students or clients still treat foresight as a menu of tools. The map comes first so later decks make sense.

So what? Start here when people ask which tool to pick. The answer is a path, not a catalog.

Houston foresight saw method lists as not enough. Managers asked where to start and in what order.

Hines and Bishop answered with six steps in sequence: Framing, Scanning, Forecasting, Visioning, Planning, Acting. This is operational practice, not random technique shopping.

So what? Treat the six pillars as a working order. Skip the order and you get tidy answers to the wrong brief.

• Framing: what problem and for whom
  • Scanning: what is changing
  • Forecasting: what futures are possible
  • Visioning: which future is preferred
  • Planning: what should be done
  • Acting: who starts today

The common mistake is jumping to scenarios or scanning because they look like the real work.

Skipping Framing, or treating pillars as optional icebreakers, produces neat answers to the wrong question.

So what? Stay on the path. Depth lives inside each column deck, not in skipping ahead.

lectureSections.title: 2. Depth of all six columns
paragraphs:
• Framing: reframing mindsets, stakeholders, intent and purpose, goal setting, team selection, strategic environment
  • Scanning: mapping, history, environmental scanning, engaging everyone
  • Forecasting: drivers and uncertainties, method choice, divergence, convergence, alternative futures

• Visioning: identifying implications, challenging assumptions, visionary thinking
  • Planning: thinking strategically, developing strategic options
  • Acting: communicating results, action agenda, strategic information system, institutionalizing strategic thinking

• Framing → 7.1 Domain description
  • Scanning → 7.2 Current assessment and scanning
  • Forecasting → 7.3a Baseline future, 7.3b Alternative futures
  • Visioning → 7.4a Preferred future, 7.4b Implications analysis
  • Planning → 7.5 Options: issue or proposal
  • Acting → 7.6 Leading indicators

Each column is one card on this page. Open a column when you need teaching depth.

Keep book doctrine separate from university or industry examples. Label examples as application.

So what? Use this page as a map and router, not as the full lecture.

Weakness in one pillar breaks the chain. Strong forecasting without visioning and acting becomes a shelf report.

Strong acting on a false frame wastes urgency. Before adding more methods, find the weakest link.

So what? Diagnose the chain first. Volume of tools does not fix a broken step.

modules.title: Column 1 · Framing
modules.lectureIntro: Framing deck: six opening slides on what this column is, where it comes from, why it matters, what it means, what it delivers, and a common mistake; then each of six parts as definition, Hines bullets, and why it matters with one applied example.

lectureSections.title: 0. Opening Framing
paragraphs:
Column 1 is Framing in Hines and Bishop's six-pillar model. It is the first step in the chain, before Scanning and Forecasting.

Here you fix the problem, the people, and the working conditions. Later pillars need a shared brief they can trust.

So what? Framing delivers boundaries, mindsets, stakeholders, intent, goals, team, and an open climate for foresight work.

In Thinking About the Future, Framing is the first operational stage of strategic foresight, not an optional warm-up.

The book puts it first so the team does not collect signals or build futures for a vague or false brief.

So what? If you skip it, every later column inherits the wrong question dressed up as method.

Without clear boundaries, people, intent, goals, team, and climate, later columns answer the wrong question neatly.

Framing is purpose-led: it tests what the work is for before data and scenarios begin.

Applied example: A university says only "stop ChatGPT cheating." Framing asks whether the real issue is assessment design, integrity culture, or workforce skills, before anyone builds AI-police scenarios.

So what? Fix the brief first. Method volume cannot save a false problem.

Framing means, before Scanning starts, we make the foresight issue, its boundaries, and the room's readiness clear and shared.

In practice this looks like: a written issue and bounds, named stakeholders, tested intent, checkable goals, a workable team, and an open climate. It is a designed readiness step inside strategic foresight.

So what? Framing is not warming up the room, and it is not jumping to scan feeds or vision slogans. Ready means the brief is explicit enough to work.

Next you teach six Framing parts. Each part has a definition, Hines guidelines, and why it matters with one applied example.

  • Reframing mindsets
  • Stakeholders
  • Intent and purpose
  • Goal setting
  • Team selection
  • Strategic environment

Two failures dominate practice. First: skipping Framing because Scanning and Forecasting look more technical. Second: treating the client's stated problem as fixed and unchallengeable.

Both send the analyst into later pillars with a false brief.

So what? In column 1, make the brief explicit, testable, and owned before the signal feed begins.

lectureSections.title: 1. Reframing Mindsets
lectureSections.imageCaption: Reset how the room stands toward the future
paragraphs:
Reframing mindsets means changing how people stand toward the future before scan or forecast begins.

The analyst surfaces cynicism, overconfidence, and quiet vetoes so attitude does not kill the method in silence. Hines and Bishop treat this as part of strategic foresight, not a soft extra.

So what? Without this step, later pillars inherit a room that only hears what it already believes.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Optimism toward the future
  • Identifying biases
  • Detecting self-deceptions and external factors
  • Using the whole brain
  • Welcoming complexity
  • The influence of time and various factors on progress

Mindset work is quality control on attention. A cynical or overconfident room misreads every later pillar.

Optimism here means disciplined openness, not cheerleading. Bias checks keep external drivers visible. Complexity stops premature simplification before Scanning locks the feed.

So what? Fix how the room listens first, or later method only amplifies old beliefs.

Applied example: A mid-size factory calls every scenario workshop "negative thinking." Until that mindset shifts, Scanning only collects good news. Forecasting then collapses to one baseline.

lectureSections.title: 2. Stakeholders
lectureSections.imageCaption: Managers, staff, and the organization as distinct concerns
paragraphs:
Stakeholder work maps whose future is at stake and what each group fears or hopes.

The analyst separates managers, employees, and the organization as distinct concerns. This is not a guest list for later workshops. It is how the brief becomes organizational, not facilitator-invented.

So what? The client stays the decision maker. The foresight team brings process and challenge.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Knowing the organization more deeply
  • Understanding the concerns of managers, employees, and the organization itself
  • Not trying to turn the client into a futurist

An incomplete stakeholder map produces elegant answers to questions nobody asked.

Separate concern maps stop a generic exercise. Keeping the client as decision maker prevents foresight theater that never lands in ownership.

So what? Name who owns the problem before you design the futures.

Applied example: A hospital foresight kickoff invites only administrators. Nurses and patients never appear. The framed issue becomes "bed capacity," while the lived crisis is staffing trust and discharge pathways.

lectureSections.title: 3. Intent and Purpose
lectureSections.imageCaption: Explore futures and test the stated problem
paragraphs:
Intent and purpose fix why the project exists for the client: explore futures, improve mental models, and test whether the stated problem is the real one.

The analyst balances exploration and exploitation before Scanning locks onto a false target. This is still the cheap place to rewrite the brief.

So what? If intent stays vague, every later column amplifies noise with more method.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Exploring the future
  • Improving mental models
  • Balancing exploration and exploitation
  • Evaluating the problem presented by the organization: is it the real problem or not

Intent work is the last cheap chance to change the question.

Exploitation protects current performance. Exploration opens alternatives. If the stated brief is wrong, Scanning and Forecasting only refine a false target with more rigor.

So what? Rewrite the question here, or pay for it in every later pillar.

Applied example: A university says "stop ChatGPT cheating." Intent work asks whether the real problem is detection tech, assessment redesign, or graduate skills the labor market will demand. That reframing changes every later pillar.

lectureSections.title: 4. Goal Setting
paragraphs:
Goal setting turns Framing into a checkable project contract: what success looks like for this foresight cycle, on which horizon, with what outward focus.

The analyst separates outputs (reports, workshops) from outcomes (decisions, capability shifts). Multiple horizons stop a short KPI from posing as a foresight goal.

So what? External focus keeps Framing from becoming internal status reporting.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Defining goals in measurable form
  • Focusing on outcomes rather than outputs
  • Working across different time horizons
  • Emphasizing the external environment and the future rather than the present and the inside

Vague goals make later "success" impossible to test.

Measurable outcomes create a contract the team can audit. Horizon discipline and external focus stop the project from collapsing into workshop counts.

So what? Write goals Acting can later judge, not activities you can merely count.

Applied example: A city transport unit sets the goal as "run four foresight workshops." Reframed, the outcome is a decision rule for modal shift by 2035, with near-term milestones Acting can track.

lectureSections.title: 5. Team Selection
paragraphs:
Team selection designs who will carry Framing and the later pillars.

Strategic foresight is collective work. The mix of roles shapes which futures become thinkable. Diversity here means role, expertise, and stake, not a decorative guest list.

So what? Build interaction across functions so blind spots surface early.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • A team sport
  • Turning it into an interactive and comprehensive process
  • Involving diverse people

A solo memo cannot replace Framing.

Without cross-functional interaction, later pillars inherit the same blind spots the room already had. Diversity of stake and role widens thinkable futures before Scanning begins.

So what? Who is in the room decides which futures can even be said.

Applied example: An energy company's foresight team is only engineers. Without regulators, communities, and finance in the room, "transition futures" stay technology roadmaps and miss social license.

lectureSections.title: 6. Strategic Environment
lectureSections.imageCaption: Open climate for thinking and trials
paragraphs:
Creating a strategic environment means designing the working climate so Framing stays open.

The analyst protects unconstrained thinking and room for small tests before politics and habit close the frame. This is permission structure for inquiry, not office decoration.

So what? Early prototypes link Framing to Acting: rough probes, not only slide debates.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • An environment conducive to open, unconstrained thinking
  • Encouraging experiments and prototypes

A room that rewards only safe answers hands every later pillar a closed frame.

Open climate and micro-prototypes keep alternatives alive long enough for Scanning and Forecasting to matter.

So what? If weird ideas die in hour one, later pillars only polish the status quo.

Applied example: A bank kickoff punishes "weird" ideas in the first hour. The team later produces polished baseline forecasts. It never tests a micro-prototype of an alternative branch service model.

modules.title: Column 2 · Scanning
modules.lectureIntro: Scanning deck: six opening slides on what this column is, where it sits, why it matters, what it means, what it delivers, and a common mistake; then each of four parts as definition, Hines bullets, and why it matters with one applied example.

lectureSections.title: 0. Opening Scanning
paragraphs:
Column 2 is Scanning in the six-pillar model. It gathers and organizes what is changing inside and outside the framed system.

The point is usable evidence of change: a system map, a history check, an environmental watch, and wide engagement.

So what? Scanning is not a pile of unread clippings. It is evidence the later pillars can use.

Scanning follows Framing and feeds Forecasting.

A clear frame tells the scan what to watch. Scan findings keep the frame honest as the world moves. In operational practice, Scanning is the second activity of the framework.

So what? It is not a free research hobby beside the project. It sits between brief and futures.

We scan so foresight is not invented from opinion alone.

Mapping, history, environmental watch, and wide engagement surface change before scenarios harden. Without Scanning, Forecasting only decorates today's assumptions.

Applied example: A ministry that only reads journal papers will miss Discord student channels, startup demos, and street-level practice where weak signals often appear first.

So what? Widen the evidence before you lock a future story.

Scanning means drawing the system, learning from the past path, watching changing contexts, and bringing many voices into what counts as evidence of change.

In practice it is structured evidence work after Framing. It is not random browsing, and it is not forecasting yet.

So what? Ready for Forecasting looks like a mapped system, a history check, a living scan loop, and voices beyond the usual experts.

Next you teach four Scanning parts.

  • Mapping
  • History
  • Environmental scanning
  • Engaging everyone

Common failures: scanning without a frame (noise), scanning only comfortable sources (blind spots), or treating the scan as finished once a folder fills.

The analyst designs a living watch that can reopen Framing when the world moves.

So what? A full folder is not a finished scan. A living loop is.

lectureSections.title: 1. Mapping
paragraphs:
Mapping is the first Scanning move: draw the system under study before the signal feed floods the room.

The team needs to know what is inside the frame, what sits outside, and how parts connect. Build an integrative view with stakeholders, not only a tech diagram or org chart.

So what? Without a map, scanning becomes a pile of clippings with no place to land.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • A global perspective
  • Mapping the system under study
  • An integrative view
  • Stakeholder analysis

The map is the sorting rule for every later signal.

Without it, volume replaces judgment. Integrative and stakeholder views keep the system human and institutional, not only technical.

So what? Decide where signals land before you collect more of them.

Applied example: A food retailer maps only warehouses and SKUs. Diet culture, delivery apps, and municipal waste rules stay "outside." Scanning never sees the drivers that will reshape demand.

lectureSections.title: 2. History
lectureSections.imageCaption: Look backward carefully before novelty claims
paragraphs:
History work grounds the project in how the present period was made.

The analyst checks continuity before novelty claims, and tests whether past "innovations" created false comfort. This is a baseline integrity check, not nostalgia.

So what? Reinventing the wheel wastes the scan cycle and hides recurring failure modes.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Beginning by looking at the past
  • Not reinventing the wheel
  • Awareness of innovations that create false comfort

History prevents false novelty and false safety.

Some past fixes feel like permanent protection and hide new risk. A clean history check keeps Forecasting from treating a recycled failure as a breakthrough.

So what? Look back before you call something new.

Applied example: A telecom celebrates an old prepaid "innovation" as proof of agility. History shows the same model already failed twice under different brands. Reinventing it wastes the scan cycle.

lectureSections.title: 3. Environmental Scanning
paragraphs:
Environmental scanning is the ongoing watch of changing contexts so Framing stays honest while the brief is being written.

The analyst runs a loop: exploration, analysis, framing, application. Internal and external environments both matter. Unattractive domains and non-academic sources matter because weak signals often hide there.

So what? Scanning that stops at collection fails the column. The loop is the product.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Scanning the environment for awareness of changing contexts, including: exploration, analysis, framing, application
  • Integrating internal and external environments
  • Examining unknown and unattractive domains
  • Not all information is in the research literature

The loop is the product, not the archive.

Unattractive domains and non-literature sources are where early change often shows first. Without the loop, Framing freezes while the world moves.

So what? Keep watching, not only filing.

Applied example: A university horizon scan uses only journal databases. Student Discord servers, edtech demos, and employer hiring chats carry early AI-use norms that journal papers lag by years.

lectureSections.title: 4. Engaging Everyone
paragraphs:
Engaging everyone widens who can see and name change in the Scanning phase.

Scanning is social evidence work, not only documentary search. The analyst consults prominent and marginalized voices and designs workshops that make learning collective.

So what? Without this, the scan reproduces the center's blind spots with more citations.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Engaging everyone outside and inside
  • Consulting prominent people
  • Consulting the marginalized / outcasts
  • Designing workshops that turn learning into collective activity

Access and legitimacy from prominent voices must be paired with edge vision from outcast voices.

Collective workshops stop expert monologue from posing as shared sensing.

So what? Who you ask shapes what counts as change.

Applied example: A municipal climate scan consults only mayors and engineers. Informal settlement leaders never speak. Flood-risk maps miss the places where adaptation already fails quietly.

modules.title: Column 3 · Forecasting
modules.lectureIntro: Forecasting deck: six opening slides on what this column is, where it sits, why it matters, what it means, what it delivers, and a common mistake; then each of five parts as definition, Hines bullets, and why it matters with one applied example.

lectureSections.title: 0. Opening Forecasting
paragraphs:
Column 3 is Forecasting in the six-pillar model. It maps a spectrum of futures from drivers and tools through divergence, convergence, and alternative worlds.

The product is coherent future fields Visioning can interpret.

So what? Do not sell one extrapolated baseline as destiny.

Forecasting follows Scanning and precedes Visioning.

Scan evidence feeds drivers and uncertainties. Alternative futures become the field Visioning will interpret and prefer. In operational practice it is the third activity: structured futures work after evidence, before preference.

So what? Build possibles first. Prefer later.

We forecast to escape a single baseline story.

Without structured alternatives, planning locks onto today's extrapolation and calls it the future.

Applied example: An auto OEM that treats one EV timeline as destiny will mis-size plants, suppliers, and skills if residual uncertainty is still high.

So what? Keep more than one usable future on the table.

Forecasting means naming drivers and uncertainties, choosing fit methods, opening then focusing ideas, and building consistent future worlds.

It is structured futures design after Scanning. It is not a point prediction sold as certainty, and it is not Visioning yet.

So what? Ready for Visioning looks like explicit drivers, fit tools, opened then prioritized ideas, and several coherent worlds.

Next you teach five Forecasting parts.

  • Drivers and uncertainties
  • Choosing forecasting tools
  • Divergence: generating ideas
  • Convergence: prioritizing ideas
  • Alternative futures

Common failures: one-number forecasts under high residual uncertainty, trend lists posing as worlds, or early convergence that only dresses today's plan.

The analyst keeps alternatives usable and internally consistent for Visioning.

So what? A neat number is not a future field.

lectureSections.title: 1. Drivers and Uncertainties
lectureSections.imageCaption: STEEP, CLA depth, intersections, era turns
paragraphs:
Drivers and uncertainties open Forecasting by naming what moves the system and what remains undecided.

Widen the field with STEEP. Deepen causes with CLA layers. Look for intersections and era turns so trends are not read one by one. Separate anchors from key uncertainties.

So what? Without this field, tool choice and alternatives rest on mood.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Identifying main drivers (obvious and less visible; STEEP strategic context; challenging present assumptions)
  • Using a layered approach (CLA) for depth of change: litany, social/systemic, discourse/worldview, metaphor/myth
  • Assessing fundamental changes that reshape the usual space
  • Seeking intersections of change (Kauffman principle; trends are not isolated)
  • Seeking turning points (Era)
  • Improving decisions by reducing uncertainty (predetermined anchors versus key uncertainties)

Driver work is the decision field for everything that follows.

STEEP and CLA stop headline litany from posing as cause. Intersections and era turns break isolated trend reading. Separating anchors from key uncertainties saves effort where choice still matters.

So what? Name what is moving and what is still open before you pick tools.

Applied example: A tourism board treats "more visitors every year" as the only driver. CLA shows litany growth sitting on a fragile worldview of endless mobility. Intersections with climate and visas become the real uncertainties.

lectureSections.title: 2. Choosing Forecasting Tools
paragraphs:
Choosing tools matches method to the ambiguity of the situation.

In project practice, tool choice is a design decision inside Forecasting, not a technique collection to impress the client. Use Courtney fit, at least one formal method for transparency, and combine techniques when one lens is too thin.

So what? Wrong tool fit creates false precision.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Correct approaches and tools (Courtney framework; fit tools to the level of ambiguity)
  • Using at least one formal method
  • Matching methods to the situation
  • Combining techniques for a wider picture of possible futures

Courtney levels stop a single-number forecast when residual uncertainty is high.

One formal method aids auditability. Combining techniques widens the futures set without pretending certainty.

So what? Fit the tool to ambiguity, not to the slide that looks most impressive.

Applied example: A pharma R&D unit faces high residual uncertainty on regulation and science, yet demands a single revenue number. Fit tools shift to scenarios plus options, not a false point forecast.

lectureSections.title: 3. Divergence: Generating Ideas
lectureSections.imageCaption: Open the field before you rank
paragraphs:
Divergence generates the idea field Forecasting will later compress.

Creative stretch must come before prioritization, or the room only dresses up today's plan. Go beyond brainstorming: invert, disturb, combine rigor and affect, and let people experience the future first-hand.

So what? Premature convergence is the main failure mode here.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Stimulating new thoughts with creative tools and approaches (strategic relatives, value analysis, and similar)
  • Going beyond mere brainstorming
  • Inverting problems (assume what seems certain is wrong)
  • Seeking disruptive ideas and anti-groupthink prompts
  • Combining rigor and creativity
  • Using both analytic and affective components
  • Experiencing the future first-hand (sensory or simulation)
  • Avoiding premature convergence of ideas

A thin ideation hour produces tomorrow's status quo with new labels.

Inversion and disturbance break groupthink. First-hand future experience makes alternatives stick long enough for real convergence later.

So what? Open the field first. Rank second.

Applied example: An insurer's "ideation" hour only yields "a better app." Inversion asks what if claims contact collapses. The field suddenly includes mutual aid, embedded cover, and exit from retail brands.

lectureSections.title: 4. Convergence: Prioritizing Ideas
paragraphs:
Convergence prioritizes after divergence has opened the field.

Forecasting needs shared grounds for the next design step without treating every popular trend as destiny. Balance realism with critique. Keep skepticism toward trends.

So what? Common ground is a working agreement, not consensus theater.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Identifying and prioritizing shared grounds
  • Balancing realism with a critical stance
  • Treating trends with skepticism

Convergence without critique freezes the status quo. Critique without realism becomes fantasy.

Skeptical prioritization preserves capacity for surprise paths Visioning will need.

So what? Prioritize without killing dissent that still matters.

Applied example: A retail team ranks "same-day delivery everywhere" as inevitable. Skeptical convergence keeps it as one plausible path, not a mandate, and preserves capacity for neighborhood dark-store backlash.

lectureSections.title: 5. Alternative Futures
paragraphs:
Alternative futures are the core product Forecasting hands to Visioning: several coherent future worlds, including the chance that today's baseline is wrong.

Describe worlds, not trend lists. Use possible, plausible, probable, preferable layers. Keep wild cards. Backcast. Quality-check consistency with evidence.

So what? Thin menus starve Planning later.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Assuming the baseline is wrong
  • Exploring and building alternative futures
  • Possible, plausible, probable, preferable
  • Emphasizing plausible surprises (Wild Cards)
  • Describing how the future differs from the present (a future world, not only a trend list)
  • Working backward / backcasting from a target scenario
  • Quality control and internal consistency
  • Supporting alternatives with empirical evidence

Alternatives are the transferable field for Visioning.

Layers organize judgment. Wild cards keep surprise in the set. World description, backcasting, QA, and evidence make futures usable rather than decorative.

So what? Hand Visioning worlds it can interpret, not a trend shopping list.

Applied example: An oil major builds only "baseline" and "green transition." Without a wild-card world (abrupt trade bloc, tech leap, or social license collapse), Planning inherits a thin menu.

modules.title: Column 4 · Visioning
modules.lectureIntro: Visioning deck: six opening slides on what this column is, where it sits, why it matters, what it means, what it delivers, and a common mistake; then each cluster as definition, Hines bullets, and why it matters with one applied example.

lectureSections.title: 0. Opening Visioning
paragraphs:
Column 4 is Visioning in the six-pillar model. After Forecasting maps possibles, Visioning asks so what and shapes a preferred direction.

It delivers implications reading, assumption stress-tests, and a shared stretch vision.

So what? Planning needs a preferred path it can inherit, not only a spectrum.

Visioning follows Forecasting and precedes Planning.

Alternatives become questions and implications. A shared preferred future then guides strategic options. In operational practice it is the fourth activity: preference and meaning after futures have been built.

So what? Build possibles first. Choose direction next.

Without Visioning, foresight stays an intellectual map.

Mission, goals, effectiveness, performance, and the bottom line need a preferred path, not only a spectrum.

Applied example: After scenarios, if a ministry asks "which one is true?", Visioning redirects: which future will we aim for, and what second-order effects does that choice create?

So what? Preference is a decision, not a truth claim about which scenario is correct.

Visioning means reading implications of alternatives, challenging hidden assumptions, and building shared stretch vision on a real time continuum.

It is preference and meaning after Forecasting. It is not picking the "most probable" scenario as destiny, and it is not Planning yet.

So what? Ready for Planning looks like owned implication chains, stress-tested assumptions, and a shared stretch direction on a time continuum.

Next you teach the Visioning clusters.

  • Identifying implications
  • Challenging assumptions
  • Visionary thinking

Common failures: asking which scenario is true, smuggling today's assumptions into tomorrow's goal, or writing a wall slogan with no time continuum.

The analyst turns alternatives into owned implications and a stretch direction people can carry into Planning.

So what? A slogan is not a vision. A preferred path with owned consequences is.

lectureSections.title: 1. Identifying Implications
lectureSections.imageCaption: Futures wheel: orders and unintended effects
paragraphs:
Identifying implications turns alternative futures into questions the organization must answer, not into final answers.

Use futures-wheel thinking to track second and third order effects before a preferred path is locked. Keep long-term and unintended consequences visible.

So what? First-order hits alone are too thin for strategy.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Using alternatives to frame important questions, not as final answers
  • Considering second and third order consequences (futures wheel)
  • Attending to long term and unintended consequences

Implication chains are how preference becomes honest.

Second and third order effects change strategy. Ignoring them produces a preferred path that fails sideways.

So what? Own the chain of consequences before you lock the preferred future.

Applied example: A university prefers "fully remote degrees." First order: lower estate cost. Second order: campus services hollow EN. Third order: local cafes and student housing markets shrink. Visioning must own those chains.

lectureSections.title: 2. Challenging Assumptions
paragraphs:
Challenging assumptions makes the hidden rules of the preferred future visible so today's conventional wisdom is not smuggled into tomorrow's goal.

State assumptions explicitly. Challenge taboos. Cross-check with experts. Disciplined doubt is the method; cynicism is not.

So what? Unspoken rules will run strategy by default if you leave them alone.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Stating assumptions explicitly
  • Challenging conventional wisdom
  • Assume nothing; question everything
  • Identifying governing taboos and breaking them
  • Cross checking assumptions and validating with experts

Unspoken assumptions run strategy by default.

Taboos are often the real constraints. Explicit stress-tests keep Visioning from laundering the present into a preferred future.

So what? Write the hidden rules down, then pressure-test them.

Applied example: Leadership assumes "students will always come to campus for prestige." Stress-testing that assumption changes the preferred vision from bigger buildings to hybrid learning ecosystems.

lectureSections.title: 3. Visionary Thinking
paragraphs:
Visionary thinking builds a shared preferred future that stretches the organization while staying on a real time continuum.

Use stretch goals, appreciative leverage, Dator's law, what-if prompts, and presencing so Planning inherits a direction people can own, not a slogan.

So what? Useful statements about the future may first look ridiculous. That can be a feature, not a bug.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Creating a shared strategic vision
  • Placing the vision on a time continuum
  • Strategic goal setting as stretch goals (BHAG / stretch)
  • Positive leverage and Appreciative Inquiry (what you focus on, you get)
  • Dator's law: every useful statement about the future first looks ridiculous
  • Asking what if questions
  • Sensing and activating the emerging future (presencing)

Shared vision is collective ownership.

Stretch pulls beyond incremental plans. Dator's law protects useful-but-odd statements. What-if and presencing keep Visioning alive to emergence before Planning freezes options.

So what? Give Planning a direction people can carry, not a poster line.

Applied example: A university stretch goal: every graduate leaves with futures literacy, not only a degree. It first sounds ridiculous. Then it reshapes curriculum, assessment, and employer partnerships.

readings.text: Hines, A. & Bishop, P. (2006). Thinking About the Future: Guidelines for Strategic Foresight. Later editions 2013 to 2020.

modules.title: Column 5 · Planning
modules.lectureIntro: Planning deck: six opening slides on what this column is, where it sits, why it matters, what it means, what it delivers, and a common mistake; then each cluster as definition, Hines bullets, and why it matters with one applied example.

lectureSections.title: 0. Opening Planning
paragraphs:
Column 5 is Planning in the six-pillar model. It bridges preferred vision to strategy and tactics that can lead to action.

It delivers strategic conversation, change-or-keep choices, and a spectrum of options with contingencies.

So what? Vision becomes choosable moves, not only inspiration.

Planning follows Visioning and precedes Acting.

Shared preferred direction becomes strategic conversation, branch points, and options the organization can choose. In operational practice it is the fifth activity: translating preference into choosable moves.

So what? Prefer first. Then build a menu Acting can schedule.

Vision without Planning stays inspirational.

Planning maps from where we are to where we want to be with options the organization can actually choose.

Applied example: A "net zero campus" vision without a menu of options and contingencies becomes a poster, not a path.

So what? Turn preferred future into choosable paths with backups.

Planning means thinking strategically in cultural and social context, then developing distinctive options with contingencies.

It is translation of preferred vision into choosable moves. It is not a single locked roadmap sold as certainty, and it is not Acting yet.

So what? Ready for Acting looks like named branch points, distinctive options, and do-nothing plus contingencies included.

Next you teach the Planning clusters.

  • Thinking strategically
  • Developing strategic options

Common failures: one best plan with no contingencies, strategy as a slide pack without organizational conversation, or ignoring what must not change.

The analyst keeps a spectrum of options Acting can carry.

So what? One locked plan is brittle. A spectrum with contingencies is usable.

lectureSections.title: 1. Thinking Strategically
paragraphs:
Thinking strategically bridges preferred vision to choices the organization can make.

Strategy emerges through dialogue in a cultural and social field, not only in a slide pack from the foresight team. Identify what must change and what must not. Find critical branching points where the path forks.

So what? Emergence means co-production in talk and practice, not a memo from outside.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Strengthening emergence at the organizational level
  • Treating cultural and social environment as the primary component
  • Creating strategy depends on stimulating strategic conversations across the organization
  • Identifying what must change and what must not change
  • Discovering main strategic choice areas through critical branching points

Strategy that ignores culture and conversation will not land.

Change-versus-preserve stops total redesign fantasy. Branch points mark where Acting must later schedule real choices.

So what? Name the forks before you write the plan.

Applied example: A public university prefers digital transformation but must preserve public trust and degree legitimacy. The branch point is what to digitize versus what must stay face-to-face credentialing.

lectureSections.title: 2. Developing Strategic Options
paragraphs:
Developing strategic options turns Visioning into a menu of moves built on distinctive advantage and evaluated on many dimensions.

Include do nothing, plausible, and preferred paths, plus contingencies for surprise. Distinctiveness keeps options from becoming generic best practice.

So what? Locking one best plan is a failure mode for Acting under uncertainty.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Building fundamental strategic recommendations on the organization's distinctive advantages
  • Multidimensional evaluation of the proposed strategy
  • Considering do nothing, plausible, and preferred options when presenting choices
  • Having contingency plans for the unexpected (a spectrum of options, not lock on one best)

A spectrum of options is what Acting can actually schedule.

Do nothing is a real choice. Contingencies protect progress when the preferred path meets surprise.

So what? Give Acting a menu with backups, not one brittle roadmap.

Applied example: Preferred path: full digital overhaul. Contingency: if the budget freezes mid-year, a modular pilot on micro-credentials still advances the vision without locking the whole enterprise.

readings.text: Hines, A. & Bishop, P. (2006). Thinking About the Future: Guidelines for Strategic Foresight. Later editions 2013 to 2020.

modules.title: Column 6 · Acting
modules.lectureIntro: Acting deck: six opening slides on what this column is, where it sits, why it matters, what it means, what it delivers, and a common mistake; then each of four parts as definition, Hines bullets, and why it matters with one applied example.

lectureSections.title: 0. Opening Acting
paragraphs:
Column 6 is Acting in the six-pillar model. Forewarned is forearmed: communicate results, set an action agenda, run a strategic information system, and institutionalize foresight.

It delivers transfer, near-term moves, early warning, and recurring capability.

So what? Foresight that stops at the workshop is unfinished.

Acting is the final pillar after Planning.

Options become transferable messages, near-term moves, early-warning indicators, and recurring organizational capability. In operational practice it is the sixth activity: making foresight survive after the workshop.

So what? The last pillar is where method becomes decision routine.

Without Acting, foresight is a one-off report.

Transfer, urgency, sensing, and institutional rhythm keep strategic foresight alive after the workshop.

Applied example: A beautiful scenario deck that sits on a shelf is a failed Acting pillar, not a successful Forecasting one.

So what? Design for transfer and repetition, not archive beauty.

Acting means designing results for transfer, deciding with imperfect data, watching weak signals, and making foresight a repeated learning practice, not a single event.

It is transfer, agenda, sensing, and institutional rhythm. It is not archiving a pretty deck, and it is not reopening Framing forever instead of moving.

So what? Done well looks like audience-fit transfer, scheduled moves, watched indicators, and a futures rhythm.

Next you teach four Acting parts.

  • Communicating / transferring results
  • Action agenda
  • Strategic information system
  • Institutionalizing strategic thinking

Common failures: shelf reports, urgency without capability, dashboards nobody watches, or one annual workshop with no rhythm.

The analyst designs transfer and repetition so foresight stays alive in decisions.

So what? If it does not change a decision calendar, Acting has not landed.

lectureSections.title: 1. Communicating / Transferring Results
paragraphs:
Communicating results designs foresight for transfer into the organization's decision routines.

Move abstract futures into forms decision makers can use in their thinking style. Immerse stakeholders carefully. Modularize outputs. Transferability beats archive beauty.

So what? Provocation is calibrated to culture, not performed for effect.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Designing results for transferability
  • Arranging the message in the audience's thinking style
  • Immersing stakeholders and decision makers in alternatives for acceptance and alignment
  • Being provocative (with care; fit organizational culture)
  • Modularizing outputs: keep the good, address the bad
  • Awareness of change through experience, insight, and reframing

Untransferred foresight is unfinished work.

Immersion raises uptake. Modular outputs let decision makers keep what helps and challenge what hurts. Lived reframe is how change awareness sticks.

So what? Write for the decision maker's language, not for the archive.

Applied example: A CFO will not read a 40-page scenario narrative. A modular one-page options brief with cost gates and decision dates transfers the same foresight into budget language.

lectureSections.title: 2. Action Agenda
paragraphs:
An action agenda turns Planning into near-term moves the organization will actually schedule: urgency, better decisions, milestones, and at least one improbable idea worth a controlled bet.

Build from strengths. Decide without perfect data. Celebrate small wins toward the preferred future.

So what? The point is better decisions, not perfect foresight.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Creating a sense of urgency
  • Strengthening what the organization already does well and building from there
  • Purpose of activity: help better decisions
  • Decide without all desired data (avoid analysis paralysis)
  • Milestones toward the preferred future and celebrating small wins
  • Recommend investing at least in one improbable idea

Urgency without capability collapses.

Strength-based moves and milestones make progress visible. One improbable investment keeps the portfolio from only safe incrementalism.

So what? Schedule moves people can start, including one controlled stretch bet.

Applied example: Besides process upgrades, the agenda funds one improbable pilot: stackable micro-credentials co-designed with employers, with a 90-day milestone and a kill or scale gate.

lectureSections.title: 3. Strategic Information System
paragraphs:
A strategic information system keeps Acting alive after the workshop: foresight-aligned indicators linked to planning gates, with early warning for weak signals that would reopen Framing or Forecasting.

Seek turbulence sources and crisis indicators that are few and easy to collect. SIS must feed decisions, not fill a data lake.

So what? Unwatched indicators are decoration.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • An information system aligned with foresight and linked to planning
  • An early warning system for weak signals
  • Searching for sources of turbulence in the system
  • Indicators that signal a potential crisis
  • Indicators that are easy to understand and collect

Unwatched indicators are decoration.

Weak signals and turbulence extend Scanning into operations. Few easy indicators beat a dashboard nobody owns.

So what? Watch a short list that can reopen planning, not a vanity dashboard.

Applied example: A university watches three early-warning indicators monthly: application yield by program, employer skill requests shifting toward AI fluency, and policy drafts on generative tools. Each triggers a planning review, not a dashboard vanity metric.

lectureSections.title: 4. Institutionalizing Strategic Thinking
paragraphs:
Institutionalizing strategic thinking makes foresight a recurring capability after the first project: clear frame, futures rhythm, training, and a learning organization that can accept change.

Make the conceptual framework explicit. Repeat strategic foresight activities on a cadence.

So what? One-off success that freezes is still failure of Acting.

In practice, Hines and Bishop point the analyst to:

  • Selecting, designing, and making the conceptual framework explicit
  • Developing a futures rhythm (regular cadence of study and attention)
  • Regular repetition of strategic foresight activities
  • Training programs for institutionalization
  • In a complex environment, learning is the best approach (learning organization)
  • Shifting attitudes toward accepting change

An explicit frame stops every project reinventing method language.

Rhythm and training beat one-off reports. Change acceptance keeps Acting from freezing after first success.

So what? Build a calendar and a shared language, not only a successful pilot.

Applied example: Instead of one annual workshop, the organization runs a quarterly foresight hour tied to budget cycles, with a short internal training so new managers inherit the six-pillar language.

readings.text: Hines, A. & Bishop, P. (2006). Thinking About the Future: Guidelines for Strategic Foresight. Later editions 2013 to 2020.

modules.title: Scenarios as strategic survival
modules.lectureIntro: Session 1 of strategic scenario planning: Shell and Wack. Scenarios are for mental preparedness, not for “correct prediction.”

lectureSections.title: 1. Shell and 1973
paragraphs: Shell had built scenarios before the 1973 oil shock that treated a price shock as plausible. Value was not numeric accuracy; it was decision readiness.
Wack insisted scenarios must change managers’ mental models. If assumptions stay fixed, scenarios sit on a shelf.
A trend report locks one future; a good scenario set builds several world logics and hardens decisions against surprise.

lectureSections.title: 2. Scenario versus forecast
paragraphs: A scenario is a coherent narrative of a possible future written for a specific decision.
Without critical uncertainty, scenarios collapse into forecasts. Find two axes with highest impact and lowest certainty.
Quality criteria: internal coherence, link to a decision, and monitorable early indicators.

lectureSections.title: 3. Focal decision first
paragraphs: Schwartz: without a clear focal decision, scenarios are entertainment.
Example: “Should the organization build a proprietary LLM by 2029 or stay on external APIs?”
Each group writes one focal decision for the term project and critiques it in class.

lectureSections.title: 1. Choosing axes
paragraphs: Axes need high impact and low certainty. A certain trend is a weak axis.
Common mistake: “low/high economic growth” with no link to the decision. An axis must change world logic.
Energy example: energy transition speed × open/closed geopolitics. AI example: regulation speed × model-market concentration.

lectureSections.title: 2. Building the 2×2
paragraphs: Each quadrant is a world logic, not label A/B/C/D.
Names should be memorable: “fossil island,” “tech leap,” not “scenario 1.”
Coherence: there must be a path from today to that future. Internal contradiction = weak scenario.

lectureSections.title: 3. Class workshop
paragraphs: Groups build two axes for the M1 decision and write four names.
Each group narrates one quadrant in three minutes.
Critique: are axes truly independent? Do names carry logic or only color?

lectureSections.title: 1. Early indicators
paragraphs: Without indicators, scenarios stay stories. Indicators show which world logic is activating.
A good indicator is seasonally monitorable, linked to an axis, and hard to game in the short term.
Example: share of domestic GPUs in government procurement, or GenAI copyright cases in key courts.

lectureSections.title: 2. Implications and no-regret
paragraphs: Under each quadrant ask: if this world is true, what strategy is required?
No-regret: actions valuable across most scenarios (for example board data literacy).
What-if: options that only make sense in one extreme scenario and should be prepared, not necessarily executed.

lectureSections.title: 3. Link to the organization
paragraphs: Scenarios without a budgeting and risk link sit on a shelf. Define at least one quarterly decision gate.
In Rohrbeck language: scenarios feed prospecting; 90-day probing tests scenario hypotheses in the field.

modules.title: Scenario typologies: Godet, Bezold, and Bell
modules.lectureIntro: Session 4 shows that scenario is not one method, it is a family of methods. Godet's typology, Bezold's participatory approach, and Wendell Bell's classification help you choose the right method for each question.

lectureSections.title: 1. Why a typology is needed
slideTitles: A Shell scenario is not a policy scenario
Two core axes of the typology
The cost of choosing the wrong method
paragraphs: Shell's scenarios were built for managers' mental preparedness; a municipality's participatory scenarios are designed to build agreement among citizens. Both carry the name scenario, yet their construction logic differs.
Two common axes classify scenarios: exploratory versus normative, and qualitative versus quantitative. These two axes alone produce four main scenario families.
Choosing the wrong type carries a real cost: running a heavy quantitative process for a question that only needed a participatory conversation wastes an organization's time and credibility.

lectureSections.title: 2. Exploratory and normative in Godet
slideTitles: Exploratory scenarios: moving forward from today
Normative scenarios: working backward from a preferred future
The quantitative SMIC and cross-impact method
paragraphs: Michel Godet defines exploratory scenarios as a move from today's trends and uncertainties toward several possible futures, a logic close to Shell and Schwartz scenarios.
Normative scenarios move the other way: the starting point is a preferred future, and the question is which paths lead to it, the same logic you have seen in backcasting.

Godet and Duperrin proposed the SMIC method in 1975 for probabilistically grouping scenarios based on cross-impact among assumptions, a more quantitative cousin of the qualitative 2×2 matrix common in management classrooms.

lectureSections.title: 3. Bezold's participation and Bell's classification
slideTitles: Clement Bezold and participatory scenario building
Possible, probable, and preferable in Wendell Bell
Choosing a typology for your project
paragraphs: Clement Bezold developed participatory scenario building for policy and public health processes, where building agreement among stakeholders matters more than analytical precision alone.

Wendell Bell, in Foundations of Futures Studies, separates possible, probable, and preferable futures. This triad sharpens the question: is this scenario possible, is it probable, or is it one we consider preferable?

To choose a typology, first revisit M1's focal decision and the project's audience: a high-level strategic decision usually calls for exploratory and qualitative work, public policy for participatory work, and financial risk modeling usually for quantitative work.

modules.title: The foresight × entrepreneurship bridge
modules.visualCaption: From futures insight to business hypothesis
modules.lectureIntro: Session 1 defines Futurpreneurship: someone who both sees the future and accepts risk to build. The gap between foresight reports and venture building in FRM becomes clear.

lectureSections.title: 1. Why foresight without venture is incomplete
paragraphs: Startups without foresight are often blind: they bet on a single-line market assumption and notice surprise too late.
Futurists without venture often only report; insight never becomes a falsifiable hypothesis and a field experiment.
Futurpreneurship is what the startup ecosystem does informally, but with foresight rigor: scanning, scenarios, and Popper Diamond quality.

lectureSections.title: 2. The FRM gap and conceptual roots
paragraphs: FRM 3.0 includes Personal Futures and Genius Forecasting chapters, but a systematic bridge to startup and venture building is outside its scope.
Richard Slaughter stressed literacy and embedding foresight in society; a foresight culture is a precondition for futures-oriented entrepreneurship.
Stuart Candy's experiential futures and immersive scenarios show the bridge from foresight to action and public engagement; inspiration for tangible experiments.

lectureSections.title: 3. The five-stage cycle
paragraphs: Sense begins with weak signals and the upper CLA layers. Imagine builds a short-horizon scenario or vision: which future is worth a venture?
Hypothesize writes a falsifiable business hypothesis: if X occurs by a stated horizon, then Y customers or needs exist.
Build is the MVP and minimum-resource pilot (probing in Rohrbeck's language). Then Scale or Kill fast; foresight prevents long wrong bets.

If you only repeat growth of a known market, you are still in trend analysis, not Futurpreneurship.

lectureSections.title: 2. Hypothesis and MVP
paragraphs: Template: if [futures change] by [horizon], then [customer segment] will show payment or adoption for [value proposition]; falsified if [criterion].
An MVP must be buildable and testable in ninety days: landing page, limited pilot, or pre-sale; not a five-year research program.
In Rohrbeck's language this is probing: organized experiment with stop criteria before a large portfolio commitment.

lectureSections.title: 3. Pitch and Popper Diamond critique
paragraphs: Each group presents hypothesis, MVP scope, and falsification criteria in three minutes.
Critique with the Popper Diamond: is creativity and innovation real, or a repeat of a common market idea? How much expertise and interaction with the target user occurred?
Class close: specify Scale, Pivot, or Kill paths with the evidence expected after ninety days.

envScanning.heroSub: The systematic acquisition and use of information about events and trends outside the organization. For executives: opportunities and threats are seen before they force a decision, not after it is too late.

history.founder: Francis J. Aguilar · Chun Wei Choo
history.institution: Harvard Business School · University of Toronto, Faculty of Information
history.title: From scanning modes to organizational information behavior
history.origin: Francis Aguilar introduced environmental scanning in his 1967 Harvard study Scanning the Business Environment, based on interviews with managers about how they actually gathered outside information. Chun Wei Choo, at the University of Toronto Faculty of Information, later reframed scanning as an information behavior problem: what an organization needs to know, how it seeks that information, and how it uses it once acquired.
history.problem: Foresight courses often treat scanning as one uniform activity. Aguilar and Choo show that organizations scan in distinct, identifiable modes, and that most consequential strategic information still reaches managers through informal, personal channels rather than formal research units.
history.applications: Corporate competitive-intelligence units, government horizon-scanning offices, environmental scans in public-health and health-services planning, and the Perceiving dimension of Rohrbeck corporate-foresight practice on this site.

introParagraphs: In Scanning the Business Environment (1967), Aguilar analyzed, through interviews, how managers at large firms actually gathered information about markets, technology, and regulation. He found that this behavior fell into four recognizable modes, ranging from casual, unplanned exposure to deliberate, structured search.

Aguilar also found that most of the information that mattered reached executives through informal personal contacts rather than formal research departments, a finding later scanning research has repeatedly confirmed.

pillars.title: Undirected viewing
pillars.desc: General exposure to information with no specific question in mind: broad reading, conversation, and media, mainly to stay informed.

pillars.title: Conditioned viewing
pillars.desc: Directed but still passive exposure: the observer is sensitized to particular topics and notices relevant information without actively searching for it.

pillars.title: Informal search
pillars.desc: A relatively unstructured but active and purposeful effort to obtain specific information, for example asking a known contact or checking a familiar source.

pillars.title: Formal search
pillars.desc: A deliberate, planned effort that follows an established procedure or methodology, such as commissioned market research, to secure particular information.

envScanning.gapTitle: From Aguilar to Choo, and the fit with FRM Chapter 2
envScanning.gap: In Futures Research Methodology 3.0, Theodore J. Gordon and Jerome C. Glenn dedicate Chapter 2 to Environmental Scanning: a systematic process for gathering external information and spotting early indicators of change. That chapter, together with Hines and Bishop's Scanning pillar, describes what to scan (STEEP or PESTLE sectors, weak signals, horizon scanning). Aguilar and Choo describe how scanning happens as an information behavior. Daft and Weick (1984) reinterpreted Aguilar's typology along two dimensions, the organization's belief that its environment can be analyzed, and how actively it intrudes into that environment to test it, producing four modes: undirected viewing, conditioned viewing, enacting, and discovering. Choo, in his ASIS&T monograph Information Management for the Intelligent Organization (1995, 2nd ed. 1998) and in a widely cited 2001 article, adopted this four-mode model, relabeling discovering as searching, and traced, for each mode, the information needs, information-seeking behavior, and information use that follow. In Rohrbeck's FITness framework, this whole territory sits inside the Perceiving dimension: an organization that scans only in undirected mode has weak Perceiving, however sophisticated its scenario or roadmap work later on.
envScanning.case: A telecom operator's regulatory team only skims two trade newsletters, undirected viewing, and once a year commissions a formal spectrum-policy study, formal search, with almost nothing in between. Using Choo's model, students identify the missing conditioned-viewing and informal-search behavior, for example assigning staff to watch a named list of regulators and industry bodies, and design a lightweight weekly scanning routine that closes the gap before the next license renewal.

modules.lectureIntro: Session one separates environmental scanning from forecasting and clarifies Aguilar’s four modes with organizational examples.

lectureSections.title: 1. Scanning is not one uniform activity
paragraphs: Forecasting asks what will happen. Scanning asks what is happening outside the organization that must be seen before a decision is forced.
Aguilar showed managers gather external information with different intensity and formality; that difference changes opportunity and threat quality.
If scanning is only “reading interesting news,” the organization stays in undirected viewing until a crisis arrives.

lectureSections.title: 2. Aguilar’s four modes
paragraphs: Undirected viewing: scattered encounters without a clear question. Conditioned viewing: guided attention with preset filters such as rivals or regulation.
Informal search: active but informal inquiry, expert calls, field observation, short customer talks.
Formal search: a named project or unit with written output, time horizon, and an owner.

lectureSections.title: 3. Diagnosing the dominant mode
paragraphs: Teams place a real unit’s scanning behavior on the four modes: who reads what, where it is logged, who decides.
Often formal search exists while conditioned viewing on weak signals is missing, or the reverse.
In cloud and AI platforms, conditioned viewing on data regulation and informal search on edge-user behavior are critical.

paragraphs: Daft and Weick grade environments by analyzability: from ambiguous to clear.
The second axis is how aggressively the organization seeks information: passive versus active.
Combining the axes creates cells that align with Aguilar’s modes and guide routine design.

lectureSections.title: 2. Choo: need, seeking, use
paragraphs: Choo treats scanning as information behavior: without a defined need, seeking becomes news hoarding.
Seeking needs sources, cadence, and accept/reject criteria; otherwise conditioned viewing turns into noise.
Use means moving a signal into a decision, budget, or probe; a report without a decision owner is dead scanning.

lectureSections.title: 3. STEEP, weak signals, and FITness
paragraphs: STEEP or PESTLE is not only a topic label; it is a conditioned-viewing template so domains are not skipped.
Scanning without a weak-signal filter sees only strong trends and discovers strategic surprise late.
In Rohrbeck’s model, healthy scanning is part of Perceiving: rhythm, owner, and a link to the technology radar.
